search_bias: benchmark-design and measurement-validity first; then judge reliability, process verification, downstream-valid reward-model evaluation, and uncertainty calibration

sources_checked.title: LiveBench: A Challenging, Contamination-Free LLM Benchmark
ProcessBench: Identifying Process Errors in Mathematical Reasoning
Judging the Judges: A Systematic Study of Position Bias in LLM-as-a-Judge
Revisiting Uncertainty Estimation and Calibration of Large Language Models
Benchmarking Uncertainty Calibration in Large Language Model Long-Form Question Answering
Diagnosing LLM Judge Reliability: Conformal Prediction Sets and Transitivity Violations
Time to REFLECT: Can We Trust LLM Judges for Evidence-based Research Agents?

candidate_findings.mechanism: Use dynamic, recently sourced, objectively scored benchmark slices as an assurance layer separate from development-tuned evaluations.
candidate_findings.evidence: LiveBench updates from recent sources and uses objective ground truth specifically to reduce contamination and judge/crowd bias; its initial study reports top-model accuracy below 65%, preserving headroom.
candidate_findings.quantitative: top models below 65% accuracy in the reported evaluation
candidate_findings.scope: general LLM capability benchmarking across math, coding, reasoning, language, instruction following, and data analysis
candidate_findings.uncertainty: Does not by itself solve open-ended agent evaluation where objective ground truth is unavailable.

candidate_findings.mechanism: Meta-evaluate judges using controlled, localized interventions that create verifiable reasoning/tool/evidence/report failures rather than relying only on human preference correlation.
candidate_findings.evidence: REFLECT constructs fine-grained process/outcome failures by controlled interventions on quality-screened research-agent traces; even the best judges remain below 55% overall accuracy, with evidence verification especially weak.
candidate_findings.uncertainty: Need category-level breakdown and intervention recipes before claiming transfer to other agent families.

candidate_findings.mechanism: Attach per-instance judge reliability diagnostics using transitivity tests and calibrated prediction sets instead of only aggregate judge accuracy/correlation.
candidate_findings.evidence: On SummEval, aggregate directed 3-cycle rates were only 0.8-4.1%, yet 33-67% of documents had at least one cycle. Conformal set width correlated with error/difficulty (Spearman +0.576, N=1,918, p<1e-100) and had cross-judge agreement around 0.32-0.38.
candidate_findings.quantitative: 0.8-4.1% aggregate cycle rate; 33-67% documents with a cycle; r_s=+0.576
candidate_findings.scope: NLG evaluation on SummEval with four judges/four criteria
candidate_findings.uncertainty: Requires testing on agent traces and binary/pairwise decision settings.

candidate_findings.mechanism: Treat evaluation quality as downstream predictive validity, not leaderboard discrimination alone; validate reward-model benchmarks against actual inference-time and training behavior.
candidate_findings.evidence: RewardBench 2 is about 20 points harder on average than RewardBench and reports strong downstream relation. In the paper's Best-of-N study across 113 reward models, benchmark-average vs downstream-average Pearson correlation is 0.87; PPO behavior is more configuration-sensitive, including on/off-policy or model-lineage mismatch.
candidate_findings.quantitative: ~20-point average score drop vs RewardBench; Pearson r=0.87 for Best-of-N downstream average across 113 RMs
candidate_findings.scope: reward-model evaluation; Best-of-N and PPO downstream uses
candidate_findings.uncertainty: High benchmark score is not sufficient for PPO quality; deployment distribution matters.

candidate_findings.mechanism: Evaluate process verifiers on out-of-distribution error-localization benchmarks and prefer data-efficient generative verification where supported, instead of trusting in-domain PRM scores.
candidate_findings.evidence: ProcessBench reports that existing PRMs often fail to generalize beyond GSM8K/MATH and can underperform prompted critic models. ThinkPRM reports outperforming LLM-as-a-Judge and discriminative verifiers using only 1% of PRM800K labels, including +8% on a GPQA-Diamond subset and +4.5% on a LiveCodeBench subset over discriminative verifiers trained on the full PRM800K; under equal token budget it reports +7.2% on a ProcessBench subset over LLM-as-a-Judge.
candidate_findings.quantitative: 1% process labels; +8% GPQA-Diamond subset; +4.5% LiveCodeBench subset; +7.2% ProcessBench subset under equal token budget
candidate_findings.scope: step-wise mathematical/reasoning verification with selected OOD generalization tests
candidate_findings.uncertainty: Results are concentrated in reasoning domains; broader tool-use/process domains remain open.

candidate_findings.mechanism: Use process-level supervision with active selection of informative steps when reliable intermediate labels are feasible.
candidate_findings.evidence: Let's Verify Step by Step reports process supervision outperforming outcome supervision on a representative MATH subset, with the process-supervised model solving 78%; it also reports active learning improving process-supervision efficacy and releases 800,000 step-level labels.
candidate_findings.quantitative: 78% on the reported representative MATH subset; 800,000 step-level human labels
candidate_findings.uncertainty: The strongest evidence is math-specific and uses costly human step labels.

candidate_findings.mechanism: Audit pairwise judges for order stability and model-family/self-style preference before using them as benchmark or training signals.
candidate_findings.evidence: The position-bias study spans 12 judges, MTBench/DevBench, 22 tasks, about 40 candidate models and >100,000 evaluation instances, finding systematic position bias varying by judge/task and solution quality gap. Separate self-preference work finds GPT-4 significantly favors lower-perplexity/familiar outputs more than humans, suggesting familiarity can masquerade as quality.
candidate_findings.quantitative: >100,000 pairwise evaluation instances in the position-bias study
candidate_findings.uncertainty: Exact mitigation efficacy needs direct ablation of order randomization, repeated trials, and cross-family judging.

candidate_findings.mechanism: Evaluate uncertainty with at least two distinct objectives—calibration and error ranking/selective risk—and avoid single-metric ECE-only conclusions.
candidate_findings.evidence: A 2025 study over 80 models finds linguistic verbal uncertainty generally stronger than token-probability and numerical-verbal methods while emphasizing that high accuracy does not imply reliable uncertainty and good calibration need not imply good error ranking. A 2026 long-form QA benchmark over up to 20 models, seven scientific QA datasets and 685,000 responses reports answer-frequency consistency as the most reliable calibration signal in its setting and warns that ECE alone can be misleading.
candidate_findings.quantitative: 80-model study; 685,000 long-form responses across seven scientific QA datasets in the 2026 benchmark
candidate_findings.scope: black-box uncertainty estimation and scientific QA
candidate_findings.uncertainty: Method ranking changes by task and response format; no universal uncertainty estimator established.

rejected_or_scoped_leads.lead: Single aggregate LLM-judge accuracy/correlation as sufficient reliability evidence
rejected_or_scoped_leads.reason: Per-instance cycles, controlled-intervention failures, order bias, and calibration gaps can remain hidden by aggregate metrics.

rejected_or_scoped_leads.lead: Reward-model benchmark score alone predicts RLHF quality
rejected_or_scoped_leads.reason: RewardBench 2 shows strong Best-of-N predictive validity but PPO is much more sensitive to policy/RM distribution and lineage.

rejected_or_scoped_leads.lead: In-domain PRM benchmark performance implies general process-verifier reliability
rejected_or_scoped_leads.reason: ProcessBench explicitly reports OOD generalization failures for existing PRMs.

rejected_or_scoped_leads.lead: ECE alone is a sufficient uncertainty benchmark metric
rejected_or_scoped_leads.reason: 2026 long-form UQ benchmarking reports misleading conclusions when ECE is used alone; calibration and ranking/selective behavior separate.

frontier: Extract REFLECT category-level failure accuracies and exact controlled-intervention construction, especially evidence-verification failures.
Test whether conformal prediction-set width and transitivity violations transfer from SummEval to research-agent judging and tool-use trace evaluation.
Collect direct ablations for judge order randomization, repeated judgments, and heterogeneous judge juries; compare reliability gain per unit inference cost.
Extract RewardBench 2 domain-wise correlations and PPO on/off-policy ablations to identify when downstream predictive validity collapses.
Search for non-math process-verification benchmarks covering tool use, code execution, retrieval, citation correctness, and long-horizon agent trajectories.
Compare dynamic contamination-resistant benchmark construction methods that preserve objective scoring while preventing benchmark gaming over repeated model-development cycles.
Investigate statistically valid certification with noisy LLM judges using small human calibration sets and explicit TPR/FPR modeling.
Compare uncertainty metrics by decision utility: abstention/selective accuracy, ranking of failures, calibration, and cost—not only ECE/Brier.

termination_diagnostics.additional_frontier_action_before_checkp: After identifying judge-bias/process-verifier leads, searched 2026 meta-evaluation work and added REFLECT plus conformal/transitivity diagnostics as a new branch.
